steps.title: Setting up DigiD in two minutes
steps.body: Install the DigiD app, link your face recognition or fingerprint, and you're set. You'll use DigiD for the Tax Office, DUO, your health insurer, and MijnOverheid, among others.

steps.title: Message box: turn on email reminders
steps.body: Go to MijnOverheid > Message box and turn on an email reminder for whenever new mail arrives. This way you won't miss a tax assessment or other deadline without having to actively check the site.

steps.title: DigiD is personal — no exceptions
steps.body: Even if you're tech-savvy: never share your DigiD details with anyone, not even 'quickly' for a parent or partner. The government will never call or message you asking for a DigiD code.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Browse MijnOverheid below and check whether your message box reminders are turned on.

steps.title: Investment fraud
steps.body: You see an ad on social media: 'Make quick money with crypto/stocks, endorsed by a celebrity.' This is almost always fake — often using a deepfaked video of a well-known face. Never invest via a link from an ad or message; always go to a recognized, regulated provider (check its official registration).

steps.title: Romance fraud and 'friendship' scams
steps.body: Someone you meet online (dating app, social media) who, after a while, asks for money — for an 'emergency', travel costs to meet you, or an 'investment together' — is almost always a scammer. Never transfer money to someone you've never met in person.

steps.title: WhatsApp fraud: 'hi mom/dad, new number'
steps.body: A message from a 'child' or family member with a new number, asking you to quickly transfer money because a payment 'isn't going through' — always verify this with a phone call to the known number, never by replying to the new one.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Check your banking app and see whether you get notified of unusual transactions.

steps.title: Phishing is getting more personal
steps.body: Classic phishing is generic ('Dear customer'). Spear-phishing targets you specifically: a message with your real name, based on info from LinkedIn or social media — for example a fake colleague, fake recruiter, or a fake delivery notice that knows you recently ordered something.

steps.title: Exercise: a parcel-delivery scam
steps.body:
Below is a recreated example of a common SMS/email scam about a 'failed parcel delivery'. Click the message to open it. There are two things you can try: click the button, or delete the email via the menu (⋮).

From: PostNL <delivery@postnl-track-parcel.info>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Delivery failed: reschedule within 24 hours

Dear customer,

Unfortunately we were unable to deliver your parcel. There is an outstanding amount of €0.49 in shipping costs. Pay this within 24 hours or your parcel will be returned to the sender.

⚠️ Just an exercise — phew!

This type of scam is hugely popular precisely because the amount seems so small (€0.49) — people think 'what harm could it do'. In reality, this steals your card details. The teacher has automatically been notified, so you can go over it together.

The warning signs:

  • The full email address isn't PostNL's: postnl-track-parcel.info
  • A tiny amount, designed to lower your guard
  • Time pressure ('within 24 hours')
  • Delivery services never ask you to pay extra online via a link

Not sure? Always go to the delivery service's own site or app by typing the address yourself, and ask family for a second opinion if in doubt.

✅ Well done!

You deleted the suspicious message without paying. Exactly right — these 'small amount' scams are specifically designed to bypass your guard.

Warning signs you spotted:

  • The full email address wasn't PostNL's: postnl-track-parcel.info
  • A suspiciously small amount to lower your guard
  • Time pressure ('within 24 hours')

Not sure about a delivery message? Always go to the delivery service's own site or app.

steps.title: LinkedIn and fake recruiters
steps.body: A 'recruiter' who reaches out with too-good-to-be-true pay for too little work, and quickly asks for personal details or a 'deposit for equipment', is a scammer. Always check whether the company really exists and whether the recruiter has a verified profile with a shared connection.

lessons.title: Check whether your data has already been leaked

steps.title: Have I Been Pwned: check it yourself
steps.body: In virtually every major data breach (LinkedIn, Adobe, various web shops), email addresses and sometimes passwords eventually end up on haveibeenpwned.com — the international standard for checking whether your data was included. Enter your email address and you'll immediately see which breaches you appear in.

steps.title: Check Je Hack from the Dutch police (optional)
steps.body: The Dutch police offer a similar, official check called Check Je Hack. Entirely optional alongside Have I Been Pwned, but a good second check from another official source.

steps.title: What it means if you show up
steps.body: Are you on one of these lists? Then there's a demonstrably higher chance of receiving targeted phishing and scam messages via email, text, or WhatsApp — your address is marked as 'active' to criminals working with leaked lists. Respond by: changing the password of the leaked account right away, turning on 2FA wherever it isn't already, and staying extra critical of unexpected messages going forward.

steps.title: Ongoing monitoring
steps.body: Some password managers (like 1Password and Bitwarden) have built-in breach monitoring, which automatically warns you as soon as one of your saved accounts shows up in a new breach — more convenient than checking manually every time. We'll cover this further in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Password managers and 2FA as the default

steps.title: Why this isn't a 'nice to have' anymore
steps.body: With dozens of accounts (work, social media, shops, subscriptions), memorizing a unique, strong password for every site by hand just isn't realistic anymore. A password manager (like Bitwarden, 1Password, or your browser's built-in one) is now standard equipment.

steps.title: Passkeys: the password's successor
steps.body: More and more services (Google, Apple, banks) now support passkeys: logging in with your fingerprint or face, no password needed. This is more secure than a password, since there's nothing that can be stolen via a phishing email. Turn this on wherever you can.

steps.title: 2FA via an app, not SMS
steps.body: For 2FA, prefer an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy) over SMS — SMS codes can be intercepted via 'SIM swapping' (your number gets taken over by a scammer).

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Check one of your most important accounts (email, bank) to see whether app-based 2FA is set up, and turn it on if it isn't yet.

lessons.title: Recognizing identity theft and social engineering

steps.title: What is social engineering?
steps.body: Social engineering means manipulating people into giving up confidential information — often by putting you under pressure, creating urgency, or making you believe the sender has authority (your boss, the bank, the police).

steps.title: 'CEO fraud' at work
steps.body: A message or email that appears to come from your manager, asking you to quickly and discreetly make a payment or buy gift cards, is a well-known scam targeting employees. Always verify via a different channel (call your manager) before doing anything.

steps.title: What to do if your identity is stolen
steps.body:
1. Change your passwords immediately, starting with your email
  2. Report it to your bank if financial details are involved
  3. File a police report
  4. Check MijnOverheid for unfamiliar entries under your name

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Think about it: would you immediately believe a message from 'your manager' urgently asking for gift cards, or would you check first with a phone call?
